utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Initially this morning we are to take evidence by videolink from Dr. Blum. If the videolink is connected, we may be able to see the doctor and hear him. Good evening, Dr. Blum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for staying up to this hour, and we will take evidence from you now. You will understand this evidence is additional to your report, the report which you signed with other doctors and which we have received and been able to study. Now, from time to time during this period, we will be having discussion with counsel, so if we appear to ignore you for a short while, please understand and don't be offended. And the first of those occasions arises now. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Before we start today, I would like to kindly ask the Trial Chamber to decide about today and tomorrow concerning the expert reports of the Prosecution and the expert reports that the Defence presented to the Trial Chamber. Could that discussion please be in closed session. The reason is self-evident, Your Honours. These are profoundly personal matters that have to do with our client, and it seems to us that discussing such problems in detail in public would not be appropriate. Also, we would like to point out that the practice of the International Tribunal, to the best of our knowledge, has been such in respect of such hearings that such debates were heard in closed session or private session. Of course I can elaborate further, but I would not want to go into all of that right now this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Petrovic, it is your motion that the whole of the evidence should be taken in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll if -- if you have no objections, Your Honour, I'd ask Mr. Re to make the submissions this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I move to that, there's just one issue I wish to raise, and that is Professor Matthews, one of the co-authors of the report - I understand this has been raised with you by the senior legal officer - is sitting in the public gallery. I've spoken to my learned colleague Mr. Petrovic. He doesn't object to Professor Matthews watching Dr. Blum's evidence, nor indeed would the Prosecution object to the Defence expert being in court or watching over the Internet, if she can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When are you proposing to call Dr. Matthews?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tomorrow at 12.15, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I notice we have lost the doctor during our discussion. I hope that isn't a serious problem. No, he's still there. Now, the submission about closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The submission is, the Prosecution -- the Prosecution's position is that these proceedings are extremely important ones in international criminal law terms. These are the first proceedings in which the issue of fitness or competency to stand trial has actually ever been heard, has ever been a hearing. In this sense, this hearing is quite historic, and Your Honours will be making international criminal law history in whatever judgement you come to. The Prosecution submits that there are compelling reasons why these proceedings should be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can understand our deliberation of -- on your submissions and hearing your final submissions on the matter, and our decision. What about the detail of the conditions of the accused which will be discussed by all the expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The position is it makes no difference, because ultimately in your decision, you have to refer to -- if you find the accused unfit to continue with the proceedings, you have to say why. You have to set out the underlying cause. The underlying cause, of course, will be discussed by the psychiatrist, so it's something that cannot be kept secret from the international community. I also add that I read yesterday in a newspaper that the underlying cause is already in the public domain. We saw it in a Croatian -- just excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers corrects me. It was certainly public when the accused arrived here, the application he was making, but I read yesterday on something circulated on the Internet here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't want to prolong this. We are cutting into the time we have available for the videolink and already the time we had thought to allocate to each side will have to be reduced, every minute we spend on this debate. It's one thing that there might be at large a general awareness of a question of the fitness of the accused to plead. It's another thing to have the detail of all the physiological and other aspects of his condition aired in public. I just want very quickly your views and submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to the other aspects, the Prosecution doesn't object if those parts are in closed session, but the underlying main cause which the Defence is relying upon, the Prosecution says should be heard in open session because to be part of the judgement. There's just one other issue. Mr. Petrovic referred to a practice here. I think he's referring to the practice which was in the Kovacevic hearing. I was there. What happened was a psychiatrist in a Status Conference, a court appointed psychiatrist was cross-examined in closed session about an ongoing matter, not about -- not about the final determination. So there is no practice as such. But the remainder of the Kovacevic hearing was in public, including the accused addressing His Honour Judge Orie and the Bench. Those are basically our submissions. There are compelling public reasons for most of it to be in public or open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you have not specified how you would see some division of the content, and will not that add a great deal of awkwardness to the examination and cross-examination if some subjects are to be in closed session and some in open?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, no. We do this every day, we go in and out of closed session, depending upon identity and so on. We know, Mr. Petrovic, Mr. Rodic and myself, we know when to go in and out and Your Honours do too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the evidence on all issues in open session. The issue of fitness to plead has been brought into the public arena. It should be seen to be heard and determined on that basis. Doctor, I am sorry for that delay. Is it appropriate for you to take an affirmation simply in the form of an affirmation as to the truth of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a form of affirmation in front of you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- be so kind as to simply raise your hand, your right hand. Do you affirm that the evidence you will give this Tribunal will be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. Now, we will commence by the Prosecution asking you some questions. As we go, we'll be trying to adjust the volume, because we have difficulty hearing you at the moment. But we will carry on. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Dr. Blum, can you please give the Trial Chamber your full name and your occupation.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Bennett Blum. I am a physician specialising in the field of psychiatry with subspecialties in the fields of geriatric psychiatry and forensic psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your curriculum vitae is attached to the report so I won't go into it. I understand that you have testified to a US Congress subcommittee on the area of geriatrics. Could you please briefly tell the Trial Chamber the subject of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in the late 1990s I was the only geriatric psychiatrist in the United States asked to testify before the US Senate Subcommittee on Commerce, Science and Transportation during their hearings on elder abuse and financial exploitation of the elderly. As part of that testimony, I spoke about the issue of assessing mental capacity and competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: During that time, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Go on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: During the course of my testimony, I spoke about -- I spoke about certain methods of assessing competency which have been used in a variety of circumstances and was one of several methods used for the assessment in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And have you, Dr. Blum, yourself devised a test for assessing competency or functionality in aged people?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where is this published?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: This is published in the 7th edition of the Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry. There is a chapter entitled "Legal Issues in Geriatric Psychiatry." I was the co-author of the chapter in the 7th edition. I am the sole author for the chapter coming out in the 8th edition, which will be released later this year. That textbook is used by every medical school and psychiatry training programme in the United States, and it's my understanding it's used by the majority of such programmes throughout the Western hemisphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about your test? Is your test in use in the United States and other countries?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is currently in use throughout many jurisdictions in the United States, at all levels. It's also being used in Spain and - excuse me - and in Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What are the features of this test that you have devised?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The protocol looks at a number of cognitive functions and behaviours to help assess -- to help assess a person's functional ability in real-world situations. Once that is done, then a more traditional medical evaluation is performed to help clarify the reasons for any noticeable impairments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please list for the Trial Chamber the things on your protocol, the features of your protocol.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The protocol as it is -- as it is now taught contains 16 variables and is easily remembered by the acronym PARADISE, in which each letter stands for two items. To quickly run through them, the letter P stands for caparison to past behaviour. It also refers to knowledge of pertinent parties. The letter A refers to alertness, attention, ability to handle abstract concepts and consideration of alternatives.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please slow down a little for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Should I repeat anything that I've just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. We have that, Doctor. But could I ask the court officer who is with you to get you a glass of water. I think it might help you during this session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In the United States] He already has it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To continue, then: With this acronym, the letter R refers to remembering, or, in other words, memory. It also refers to the understanding of responsibilities. The letter D in the acronym refers to both the presence of delusions, which is a psychiatric term referring to fixed or unwavering false beliefs that are not appropriate or consonant with the person's culture, background, or education and are maintained despite contrary evidence. The letter also refers to the issue of impairment in decision-making abilities. The letter I refers to the presence of illnesses, which includes medications, and it also refers to the issue of the impact or the person's ability to understand the impact of their decision, meaning the likely objective consequences. We are almost completed. The letter S refers to the significance of the behaviors, meaning that person's emotional understanding of their decisions. And the letter also refers to the ability to strategise. Finally, the last letter, E, refers to the effect of emotions, and it refers to the questions of the person's ability to express their desires.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Moving to the report which you and Professor Matthews and Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc prepared for the Prosecution in this matter, I'm going to ask you about the methodology the three of you adopted in assessing General Strugar. Could you please briefly explain the methodology you adopted.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. The methodology involves several components. In brief, we reviewed the existing documentation regarding General Strugar's health and assessment of his emotional and cognitive abilities. We then performed a general psychiatric evaluation, which included testing of various brain functions in order to render a diagnosis. With regard to the questions that we were asked for this hearing, inasmuch as we were asked to assess his ability to function in a number of ways that are listed on the front page of our report, we looked at his functional abilities using the PARADISE 2 model that I have just enumerated for you, as well as a model for assessing trial competency, which is used in - excuse me - which is used in the United States, several places in the United States, and we also answered specific questions that were provided to us by the Prosecution team. These are all listed -- those questions and the responses are listed on pages 17 and 18 of our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you -- did the three of you divide the work you did and the parts of the report you wrote between you?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc do the initial part of the report which refers to the detailed history-taking, and did you do the part under the heading at page 13 -- I'm sorry, page 9, "Functional Abilities," from page 9 to page 13, and did Professor Matthews basically author the part on trial competency abilities, from page 13 through to page 16?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. The one thing that I would add is there is a paragraph immediately above the heading of "Functional Abilities" on page 9 which I authored. But otherwise, you are -- your description is accurate. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Taking you to something specific in the report at page 3, it's under the heading of "Review of Pertinent Records" on page 2, and it's the sixth line down in the first paragraph on page 3. The report said: "Conceptual remembering is not compromised." That's one sentence. The next sentence says: "Executive functions are preserved." I want you to explain to the Trial Chamber what each of those two sentences means. That is, what is conceptual remembering and what is executive functions?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Conceptual remembering is a term that is not commonly used in psychiatry in the United States. However, it refers to the ability to recall pertinent information and in abstract terms. To remember -- in other words, to remember concepts. Executive functions refer to the ability to manipulate and use those abstract concepts and that memory in order to plan, consider likely options and consequences, initiate behaviour, monitor one's behaviour, and carry things out, in other words, to strategise and to complete an action based on one's decision. These -- all of the information in this paragraph came from a neuropsychological report from the Institute of Neurology of the Clinical Hospital of Serbia, dated October 2nd, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please give us a concrete example or practical example of each of the two things; that's conceptual remembering and executive functions.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Well, as we know, later on in our report, we talk about -- on page 9, I speak about the issue of abstract concepts, and here this would be the equivalent of the -- this would fall under both categories, the conceptual memory and the executive functions. For example, General Strugar was able to correctly use and describe many abstract concepts, including the issues of guilt versus innocence, the roles of his attorneys, the role of the Judges and of the Prosecution, the purpose of the United Nations, and the concept of leadership responsibility. We go on for several pages, but what is written in the report on those pages is a more complete answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your report refers to your interviewing General Strugar and the presence, of course, of a native speaker for him, Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how it worked with her and the interpreters speaking to him in Serbian, or Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc sat at one end of the table and the general sat across from her. Physically next to her sat Dr. Matthews, and I sat next to him. And then off to my left and also sitting just to the right of General Strugar was an interpreter. As Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc spoke, as she conducted her interview, the interviewer -- sorry, interpreter, rather, simultaneously translated their conversation. There were times when Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc disagreed with a translation and at which time she would pause the proceedings and elaborate to Dr. Matthews and myself what her disagreement was and how she thought the specific phraseology should be translated. This happened primarily with issues involving detailed psychiatric symptomatology.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Dr. Blum, your report also refers to your interviewing people at the prison. Why did you speak to prison guards and nurses about the general?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Whenever involved in litigation, it's important to obtain as much objective information as possible, and so I interviewed people who had no personal stake in the outcome of this hearing. And as we noted in our report, both the nurse and one of the correctional officers had supported the self-report of General Strugar that he had decreased or impaired memory. This became very important and a much more substantiated issue for us to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's also been an issue of an MRI, and I think you spoke to Dr. Pressman, a specialist in the field of neuroradiology. What significance, if any, did the MRI have to your findings?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The MRI was - excuse me - there was an MRI performed back in 2002 which provided a biological basis for concluding that the general had vascular disease that was affecting different parts of his brain. There had been a conclusion that he suffered from a dementia that was caused by these problems. As a result of our interview and the observations from objective individuals, we also concluded that it was likely that he had a dementia probably correctly diagnosed as being caused by a vascular disease. The MRI performed in 2004 was in fact performed to help verify and confirm the earlier MRI findings. We did not have the original films to look at, we only had a report, so the 2004 MRI was performed, and in my conversation with Dr. Pressman --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Doctor, can you just very briefly just say what the significance, if any, of it was. We're running short.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Basically, the 2004 MRI did not reveal the presence of any major strokes or Alzheimer's disease and in fact if the general is in fact suffering from dementia, it would be of very mild severity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, this is my final question. It relates to psychological testing. Dr. Dusica Lecic-Tosevski's report refers to four different types of psychological testing: The symptom test check is 90 Revised. That's the SCL-90-R. The Impact of Events Scale, that's the IES; the Hamilton Scale for Depression, that's the HAM-D; and the Beck Depression Inventory, the BDI. Your report doesn't refer to your doing any of that testing. What is the significance of this testing and why didn't you perform it? As briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Those tests are used in clinical settings and are known to have very limited usefulness in a forensic evaluation. In fact are incorrect a significant percentage of the time. Also, most, except for the HAM-D are based upon self-reports and again, whenever assessing a litigant, a self-report is considered a slightly lower degree of importance or veracity than is independent and objective information by others. Third, those tests, even if -- even though they were never designed to make diagnoses, but rather to help monitor the progress of treatment, they do not assess the -- they cannot assess to what extent any diagnosis actually interferes with the person's real-world functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That's my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Re. Doctor, we will now ask Defence counsel if there are questions they wish to put to you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Blum, I am attorney-at-law Mr. Petrovic. I represent the defence of General Strugar and I will be asking you certain questions regarding your report. Would you be so kind as to tell us, based on what criteria did you and your colleagues divide tasks? In other words, could you explain how did you compile this report? In which way?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The tasks were -- it was decided that Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc would conduct the majority of the interview because of her familiarity with the language, and also for that same reason that she would -- that she would write the section of the report dealing with the background and information obtained from General Strugar during that interview. Because of my expertise in assessing cognitive abilities in the elderly, I performed that portion of the examination and wrote that section of the report. The issue -- the section labelled "Trial Competency Ability" and the assessment that was used there was performed by Dr. Matthews, as he was the most familiar with that particular protocol. We all participated in answering the questions indicated at the back of the report on pages 17 and 18 and in preparing the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you draw up those conclusions? Did you do that while you were here in The Hague or did you do it differently? Just try to be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: We certainly held discussions while we were still in The Hague. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Then the actual writing of the conclusions took place after we had all returned to our respective homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this case, did you apply the test that you have discussed today here, the PARADISE test?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us, because at least I, reading your report, did not manage to find the place where it says that the test that you have devised was applied and that it is applied in your practice. Where does it say so in the report?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: That is referenced on page 9 of the report under the heading of "Functional Abilities." There's a sentence stating "These were assessed according to a standard format developed by Dr. Blum," and there's a citation listed in there. We did not list all of the places where that is -- where that material is published. The results of that protocol are found both in the section labelled "Functional Abilities" and also woven in other parts of the report. I try to not list things out in an artificial manner, saying -- so, for example, I thought it much easier to include information regarding his medical history under the common and appropriate section, labelled "Medical History," rather than repeat essentially the same information later and say -- and notate that that was one of the 16 items that I considered. The remaining -- many of the other items are listed on basically pages 9 through the top of page 13, and you'll see that often times several are -- several of the factors are put together because -- basically for ease of understanding and communicating the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We did not really understand each other, but it doesn't matter that much. Tell me, please: On page 2, you say that out of all the medical background material that you had at your disposal, you used only those that relate to trial competency. Tell us, please: Why did you leave out of your analysis all the other material regarding the health condition of the accused and which, as we are informed, had been placed at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I'm not sure what information you are referring to specifically. However, I and Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc and Dr. Matthews were of the same opinion that there were certain aspects of General Strugar's medical history which were not germane to the issue of trial competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Blum, from the documentation that was given you, we can see that the general suffers from bilateral nephritic necrolysis, chronic kidney insufficiency, spondylosis, and various other disorders affecting kidneys and the backbone. All this is left out in your report. These disorders do affect, however, the overall health condition -- his overall health condition and his mental condition.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Well, I would agree that he has those conditions and that they affect his overall health. However, the basis -- however, the findings of our evaluation was that they did not specifically impact upon his cognitive abilities nor his -- or even more specifically, his ability to knowingly and -- knowingly and reasonably participate in these hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it is your position that you assessed those diagnoses and that they do not have any effect on his trial competency?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Not at this point in -- it's my opinion that they do not have an effect at this point in time. Clearly, there was a concern that should these conditions significantly worsen, that that assessment may change.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that chronic nephritic insufficiency, which the accused Strugar suffers from as a diagnosed disorder, has a strong effect on his capacity to function mentally?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Actually, it is interesting that you ask me that question, because in approximately 12 hours, I am flying to give a presentation at the American National Kidney Foundation and will be speaking about the -- in part, about the effects of kidney disease on cognitive abilities. The kidney disease may impact cognitive function; however, if someone has a chronic disorder and is stable, then what we do is assess how they are able to function. In this case, again, it is my conclusion that General Strugar retains adequate mental capacity and that would be so despite his chronic renal condition. Should that condition change, then of course it may impact his cognitive processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen the medical reports compiled over the years regarding the levels of urea and creatine relating, of course, to this particular disorder, including the recent reports dating to February this year?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I considered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the levels of urea and creatine that exist in the body of the accused, do you really believe that those levels are such that they have no effect on his functioning? And furthermore, what is the maximum level above which levels of urea and creatine would affect his mental abilities?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The levels of both urea and creatine certainly can affect cognitive functioning. Whether -- if it happened to you or me that our bodies suddenly had such elevated levels, then our cognitive abilities would likely be affected. However, among people who have chronic renal disease, those levels do not spike suddenly but rather increase over a period of time and there are many people - in fact it is very common among nephrology patients - that they will have very high levels of urea and creatine and nonetheless be able to function adequately in the everyday world or be able to function in a courtroom setting. The issue of absolute levels is one that cannot reasonably be answered, particularly when you're speaking about the -- relating a level of urea or creatine to the ability to participate in a specific act, such as this one. The effect of urea and creatine varies from person to person, so it is medically not feasible --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, if you can give me answers that would be slightly briefer, please. I would appreciate it very much if you could give me shorter answers, because we are under very tight time limitations, in principle.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I will do my best. To quickly finish my answer, in brief, it is not medically feasible to look at a blood chemistry level for urea or creatine and from that be able to determine someone's cognitive abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am not saying and I am not asserting that that is the only factor, but I am asking you: Which level of urea and creatine was present in the blood of the accused at the time when you assessed him?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Offhand, I do not know, but I know what his cognitive functioning was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the value was high, low, medium, was it spiking in relation to previous tests? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Both those levels can fluctuate depending on a variety of circumstances. The only way to know would have been to have conducted that blood test on the days that we interviewed him. That wasn't done, at least not to my knowledge. But again, the issue is how was he able to -- for me, the issue was how was he able to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: In the long run, how does chronic renal insufficiency affect the condition of the accused? If somebody suffers from this disorder for a number of years, how does that affect what is called chronic metabolic encelopathy? In the accused, for instance.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: That question can be answered only in terms of general epidemiology, so I can tell you what may happen to a percentage of the population; it is not possible to know how chronic renal disease will affect any given individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Your assertion that this -- these chronic renal disorders that are present in the accused, are they in no way related to what you established in several places in your report; his drowsiness, his disaffectedness, lack of interest in certain situations?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Each of the behaviors that you just listed are reasonably -- have multiple causes. Should his renal disease worsen, then I would say that any one of those three could also worsen. Again, in people who have chronic -- people who have fairly chronic disease, if their condition is more or less stable, you'll not see sudden changes in their cognitive Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To conclude this section: At the time when you were making your assessment, no attempt was made to measure the parameters of the renal functions in the accused was made, and you had no such data.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us very briefly: Spondyloarthrosis of the neck area of the vertebra, is it true that it can affect blood circulation and feeding of the brain in the accused also in large measure?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Again, epidemiologically, it is possible. How it affects any given individual is not possible to know without specific evaluation. If a person -- and in this, just as in chronic renal disease or indeed any chronic disorder, if the condition is not changing rapidly, then the cognitive processes will also not change rapidly. They will be stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you draw any conclusion about the influence of spondyloarthrosis in the neck area in the accused on his blood circulation and the feeding of the brain?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: My conclusions were that, regardless of his medical conditions, he retained a certain level of cognitive abilities. With regard to any specifics, such as drowsiness or somnolence, as we noted in the report, there were times when he complained that he would be drowsy, but nonetheless stayed alert and focused for very lengthy interviews, and when observed in a hearing, when he was observed to apparently become drowsy later on, a couple of hours later, he nonetheless was able to accurately summarise the testimony that had occurred during that time. So again, as a psychiatrist, I am more interested in the -- in his actual level of functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you did not assess this aspect either, nor did you have any insight into it, when making your report, namely, the spondyloarthrosis of the neck area? Briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I did not evaluate any type of arthritic disorder per se, only his overall cognitive ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you did not evaluate the influence of arthritic changes on his cognitive abilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: What I evaluated was the overall level of his abilities, as is enumerated in the report. And inasmuch as I felt that if he had any impairment, it was mild.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. Regarding PTSD, have you seen the results, the test results produced by Dr. Lecic a few weeks prior to your talks with the accused? And if you have, do you have any comment on the way these tests were done?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I saw her report and some of the details that she included in her report regarding those tests. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Then, yes, I did see those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you have any comment on the way the accused was tested for PTSD in terms of methodology and in terms of results?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. The PTSD stands for post-traumatic stress disorder. The test he was given was the Impact of Events Test, and in fact it was indicated that he was given the 1979 version. I was surprised that that version was used for a couple of reasons. First of all, it never was designed to diagnose PTSD. It is used to assess the degree of two symptoms, the symptom known as avoidance and the symptom known as intrusions, both of which can relate to a number of disorders. Also, the test has been significantly revised. In fact, I was -- I would have expected that at least the 1995 version would have been used, not the 1979 version. The test was revised because there were significant problems with the older version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Dr. Blum. Tell me: Which test did you apply? Did you apply any test at all during the entire course of your evaluation of General Strugar, except the procedure of interview? Did you use any other method in your interview except free-style discourse?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Well, our discourse was not free-style, so I think that's a misrepresentation. But in addition to interviewing him, observing his reactions and obtaining information from outside sources, we also specifically asked him a number of neuropsychiatric questions that assessed different parts of his brain and the functioning. And the results of that can be found -- I will tell you on what page in a second. The results of those tests can be found on page 9, the middle paragraph that begins with the words "Upon direct questioning..." And as you will see there, we assessed, at least briefly assessed, immediate recall and short-term memory, orientation, the ability to name and therefore use language, the ability to maintain alertness and attention, and other executive function, general knowledge levels, and the ability to read and the ability to deal with at least two-dimensional -- correction: two-dimensional geometric shapes, each one of which assesses a different lobe or area of the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So as far as depression is concerned and PTSD, you did not use any other diagnostic instrument except for clinical interview? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: We used the information obtained from interviewing both General Strugar and others and compared it to the diagnostic criteria in the DSM-IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to paragraph 9 later, but let us move on rapidly now. In relation to the brain MRI, is it correct that in your statement you established that the quality of that image, which was done in March, was inadequate, was of poor quality, March 2004?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: It was -- according to my understand -- according to what Dr. Pressman had told me, was that it was inadequate to assess the small deep blood vessels, which are often affected in cases of vascular dementia. However, the study was adequate to indicate that there was no major anatomical damage. And of course -- the conclusion -- that we -- that we said that he in fact does suffer from a dementia due to vascular disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 16 of your report, it says that the quality of the MRI that was done in March 2004 does not allow for an appropriate evaluation of the small, deep blood vessels that are usually affected in cases of vascular dementia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. I had just said that in my last response. Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that your overall assessment of the changes on the small blood vessels of the accused, and these changes are typical of vascular dementia, that this overall assessment was made and that actually you did not have full insight into the kind of changes that exist from that point of view?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The conclusion was based upon the previous MRI plus the impairments that we noted or that were noted by others. Everything was consistent with the issue of vascular dementia. The alternative would have been to rely solely upon -- if we had relied solely upon the 2004 MRI, then we would have had to say that there was no obvious anatomical damage. It was my feeling that the part of that study that was poor may obscure areas of actual damage that were -- that showed up in the 2002 MRI.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: In case of such ailments, changes between 2002 and 2004, are they possible at all? That is the first part of my question. And the second part of my question is: Are these changes an improvement in the condition of the small, deep blood vessels in the brain or is the only prognosis actually further deterioration of the condition that has to do with the functioning of the small blood vessels of the brain?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Over time, the damage to blood vessels will -- generally worsens. It is not possible to predict in advance how quickly that progression will occur; it varies from person to person. So from 2002 to 2004, if there was a change, then it would have been for the worse. And the only -- the -- and again, we would be looking at the impact on the general's actual ability to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: This part of your report that is called the Narrative Summary of the report, that is, from page 5 onwards, that is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. actually the content of your interview with the accused; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During the interview that you had with the accused, did it seem to you at any point in time that what he was saying was naive in a way for a man of his age and with his life experience? Did you perhaps gain that impression during the interview?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: No. In fact, if there was -- if anything, many of his responses indicated that he is an extremely intelligent and socially acute individual. In other words, many of his responses were quite sophisticated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Some of the explanations he gave to you, do they seem totally inappropriate to his position and his education and the social standing he had before?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: No. We saw no such inappropriate behaviour or response.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that he could not remember even your names after having talked to you for a few hours?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: He did -- it's correct, he did not remember the names. He remembered topics of conversation, he remembered specific things that individuals had either --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be specific and answer my question. Is it correct that he could not even remember your names after having talked to you for a few hours? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: He did not remember -- well, correct, he did not remember names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you applied some tests as well and that the only tests you did apply are in the second paragraph on page 9 of your report. Now, in relation to the first test that you conducted, there were three brief phrases that you proposed to him. You asked him to remember them, and he could not remember two out of three; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us: As for the rest of the questions you put to him, during that part of the test you asked him about the most elementary things that have to do with names of parts of the body, the day, month, year, and so on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. These are standardised questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you put any questions to him that were remotely more complex in terms of this testing, apart from recognising parts of the body, the day, month, year, and so on, in this part of your test, the one that is referred to on page 9, paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Well, he was asked significantly more difficult questions throughout two days of interviews, and the results of those are found elsewhere in the report and they are not indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about the clinical interview. I'm asking you about this part of your testing that is in paragraph 2, page 9. Could you please be as brief as possible, because our time is running out.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The purpose of this type of testing was to give the standardised questions that would indicate the presence of -- or correction: that would be used just for a cursory overview of the neuropsychological functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, when a patient cannot remember two out of three notions? What is your assessment then of his capacity to remember, his memory? And, on the other hand, there is the clinical interview that you conducted in relation to the accused Strugar.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: What it means is determined upon caparison between the performance of that question versus the remainder of the interview. Inasmuch as the general was able to recall - correctly recall - many items of great sophistication and in significant detail when they were in a context that was germane to his present situation, then I put very little emphasis upon his inability to remember a couple of random -- or correction: unrelated and contextually -- unrelated statements not put into a personal context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the accused is expected to remember different new types of content for five hours a day, things he hears in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: What I know is that he certainly demonstrated that ability in terms of the second day of our interview, when he was able to correctly recall testimony that he had heard several hours before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would you agree that we take a short break now, in view of the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Petrovic. But we will ask you to draw your cross-examination to a conclusion in another three minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to say that with regard to an 18-page report, I managed to cover only a minimum of a minimum. But if it is so, I have no choice but to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Blum, that you established that General Strugar is affected by vascular dementia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Also, very briefly: Is it correct that vascular dementia, that is one of his illnesses, affects the memory of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: By definition, all dementia, regardless of the cause, affects memory. So yes. The major issue is matter of degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that his memory is decreased and that he has difficulties related to that?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes, to a mild extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he has other cognitive parameters that are also reduced, as stated on pages 17 and 18 of your report?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. And actually, I would -- actually, I would correct that by saying they are stated on page 16 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there is a significant number of vascular dementia patients who are unfit for trial?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Of course. Again, that's a question that looks at general population, not a specific individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When looking at his condition, do you find any restrictions in terms of his ability to follow the trial before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: No, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it your claim that General Strugar can follow these proceedings under the same conditions that a completely healthy individual can?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to elaborate what that means, "In general, yes."

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: What that means is that it's my opinion that he understands the charges against him, he understands the nature and process of the proceedings, he's able to interact with yourself and co-counsel, he's able to testify, he's able to remember and evaluate the testimony of other witnesses. He's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, please. My question is whether this man, Pavle Strugar, can follow these proceedings, this trial, under the same conditions that a totally healthy individual man can. I did not ask you about what you were saying now in your answer.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I apologise if I misunderstood your question. My conclusion is: Yes, he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that Pavle Strugar is a healthy man?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I believe he has a number of medical problems, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that he is a healthy man?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: That depends on how you're going to define the word "healthy." If you mean absent of any medical conditions, then no, he is not. If, however, you mean able to function despite having medical conditions, that relative degree of health, then yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a multitude of questions pertaining to this report. However, in view of the limitation that you imposed upon me, I am not in a position to put the remainder of my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. As you'll appreciate, we did allow you quite some flexibility with time there. Mr. Re, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are several matters which I would wish to clarify with the doctor, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have a very limited time in which to do it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Dr. Blum, several matters arise which I wish to clarify. You spoke about the PARADISE test and how you had referred to several of those issues at pages 9 to 13 of the report. I just want you to please list -- just list the headings as they relate to the PARADISE report, PARADISE -- sorry, test, 16 issues.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: All right. The headings would be, as they're listed in the report, Abstract Concepts, then on page 11, "Understanding of potential consequences; consideration of alternatives; objective impact of outcomes; subjective meaning of outcomes." Next is the Ability to Remember Information; next is the heading of Attention and Alertness; and then, on top of page 13, there are a number -- a number of factors that are further listed under the heading of Assessment of Cognitive Abilities. And those include the ability to strategise, correct recognition of pertinent parties in the current litigation and their responsibilities, the ability to make decisions, the ability to express desires, and the lack of any delusions, as I had defined the term earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic also asked you about a sentence in paragraph 2 of page 9 about General Strugar's inability to remember two out of three things which were read to him. You used the words in your report that he was claiming that he could not remember the other two. Why did you use the word "claiming" in that context?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Because -- I used the word "claiming" because throughout the interview, the general evidenced many times in which he was able to remember -- he was able to remember quite sophisticated questions, phrases, witness testimony, et cetera. And so when he said that he could not remember, that is what I documented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic also asked you about General Strugar not remembering your name during the interview. How did -- sorry. How did General Strugar refer to the three of you? What did he call you?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: He would -- he either would look directly at one of us and begin speaking. I believe he remembered Dr. Folnegovic-Smalc, which is not surprising, since the majority of the time was spent speaking directly to her. And so I was not at all surprised that he did not remember my name or that of Dr. Matthews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic also asked you about the diagnosis in Dr. Lecic-Tosevski's report of post-traumatic stress disorder. And you referred to your referring to the DSM-IV criteria. I don't think it's referred to in your report. Can we take it that it is the same criteria she refers to at page 11, that is paragraph 309.81 of the DSM-IV, or were you referring to a different criteria? If you can't say it offhand, abandon it.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: I have a copy of the DSM-IV here. Tell me the page number again, please.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes. Well, 309.81 is the code for post-traumatic stress disorder. That is found on page 468 of the DSM-IV text revision. Correction: technically, there's a couple of lines that begin on the bottom of page 467 and continue on page 468. In answer to your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that what you were referring to? That's all I'm asking. Or is it a different paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Blum, Mr. Petrovic asked you directly whether General Strugar suffered from vascular dementia, to which your answer was yes. Your answer "yes" to that question, does it have to be read in the context of the conclusion of your report, quote at page 16: "It is our opinion that the defendant's cognitive impairments are sufficiently mild that they do not prevent him from understanding the current proceedings and assisting in his defence." And two paragraphs down: "In this case, the defendant has mildly decreased memory and occasional word-finding difficulty." Does your answer "yes" have to be read in that context?

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There is a difference between the diagnosis and the question of the severity of someone's condition. And so yes, context is essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Doctor, Mr. Petrovic -- or you answered a question in relation to Dr. Lecic-Tosevski's use of the 1979 IES, and you said there were some problems, significant problems with it. Are you able to very, very briefly tell the Trial Chamber what the significant problems were and why you wouldn't use this test now.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: The test was -- the test was never designed to make a diagnosis of PTSD but, rather, was designed to help assess various subcomponents, certain symptoms that are found in PTSD plus in other conditions. That test is not used in litigation settings in general because it -- because the reliability is fairly low. Actually, under the -- various studies of the reliability suggest reliability of anywhere from approximately -- well, I should say at least 25 per cent error on up to -- on down to about a 10 -- 8 to 10 per cent error rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Blum.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: For litigation, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if you wish to complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: BENNETT BLUM
utterances.text: No. I was going to -- I was going to say that for litigation purposes, it is much -- it's much more important to rely upon the DSM-IV diagnostic criteria plus an assessment of actual functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Re. Doctor, we are very grateful for the time you've made available and the inconvenience which you have experienced. That concludes the time we've allocated for evidence. So we thank you and wish you a good night's sleep. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now, to resume at 10.00, when we hear submissions from the Croatian ambassador with respect to the Defence motion for documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be followed by a Motion Hearing. The hearing will reconvene at 11.02 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I just make an indication to the Chamber that the Prosecution and the Defence have spoken about the document under tab 3, which Your Honour had instructed us to discuss, and the Defence has indicated that for this harbour-master's log, as we call it, they would like to have, rather than the entire volumes, the dates of 5 December through 20 December. And we are working with the particular entries that are in whatever is in tab 3. And I would -- accordingly, that was the basis for our holding out trying to get it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are now proceeding to prepare the whole document, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Defence has asked for those dates, not the entire document. The entire document is quite long. But those dates -- they have the entire document but we're happy to single out those particular portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And in a day or so they will be available and you will produce them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence has indicated its willingness to assist in the copying process, so we think that -- the Defence may wish the additional dates. We are only looking at the ones that are in tab 3 right now. And accordingly, we'd ask that our particular exhibit -- that the exhibit as it stands be admitted and whatever the Defence is seeking to add could be included as part of that exhibit number, if that's satisfactory to all parties, to all persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you'd like us to receive that document now and to be prepared to add further pages to it by agreement with the Defence, as soon as those pages are available?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague opposite is nodding his head, as that is our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good. When the Prosecution and the Defence are in agreement, the Chamber moves on quickly, so that there can be no chance of a change of mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All we'd ask for is perhaps an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That's tab 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is P162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Rudolf. If we could just remind you of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yesterday, as we concluded our session, we were discussing an entry in what is Exhibit P162, Prosecution 162, which was what we've been calling the harbour-master's log. And we had looked at the dates -- well, right now the date of 5 December, as it is entered in that document. And I wanted to return -- also emphasising that when His Honour mentioned that there was confusion about where the pages numbers are, I will indicate, for purposes of today, I stand corrected, Your Honour, that we should be using the number at the upper left-hand top because they correspond both the Serbo-Croatian and the English. Apologies. And that's what we'll refer to now. Looking at -- let's see. I'll take you back to where we were yesterday. I was looking at what would be page 3 in the upper left-hand corner of everybody's. We were talking about on the 5th of December an entry anticipating the future use, on the 9th of December, 1991, of the Argosy II, the same boat we were talking about. Do you recall that's where we left off, Mr. Rudolf? I'm sorry. If you could just --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And that just to recap, the suggestion in this particular entry is that it will be used to provide Cavtat with food and medicines. Is that consistent -- do you agree that that is in fact the entry in this particular log for the day?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving along to page 6 on the 5th of December. There's an entry by 11.00, it says 11.00, and it is addressed to the Boka VPS command, protesting the acts of your units in and around the village of Bosanka, who opened sniper fire on the Old Town, wounding two civilians at 1100 hours. You had indicated yesterday that you had received reports of various incidents, shall we call them. Was this particular incident reported to you? Did this become known to you or is it simply something that made its way into the log? Was there any discussion about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was indeed informed about these incidents, but whether I was informed of this particular one, I cannot recall at the moment. But they did discuss these incidents when they explained the situation in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For just a moment, if I could ask to turn your attention to tab 8. Have you been presented with that, Mr. Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It's actually tab 8 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher is able to assist. I don't believe that the witness has the binder. Oh, it is on the screen. Okay. If we can proceed on Sanction, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is a document dated 5 December that bears the -- to the command of VPS, naval sector, from the Crisis Staff, also containing the information we just looked at, or appearing to contain that same information, about sniper attack on civilians in the Old Town. And does this appear, Mr. Rudolf, to be the same information by its description as what you've just looked at on page 6 of the harbour-master's log, what we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Reference is made here to Bosanka, which is a small hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would move this document into evidence, and at this time -- yesterday I asked for tab 17 to be identified, and I would also ask at this time that it be moved into evidence. It also involves incidents during the time period of alleged attacks on civilians. Looking at -- what is in tab 8 and in tab 17, which have been given yesterday, P161.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 17 is P161, the document dated 4th of December, and there is no English translation for that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct. We will seek one for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And this tab 17 then will be P163.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tab 17 -- just a minute. You're ahead of me there. Tab 17 at the moment is marked for identification as 161.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It has no translation, Your Honour. Tab 8 has a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now you are wanting to move firstly tab 17 into evidence now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what it says, which puts me at a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. We can repeat the contents, or perhaps I may have thought we had done it yesterday. May I ask that it be shown and read in by the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters ask that the document in B/C/S be placed on the ELMO then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is P163.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is P161, P161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tab 17 onto the ELMO, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. Registrar's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you -- Mr. Rudolf, if you'd be kind enough to read into the record -- it's a fairly brief text. The date at the top, if you could, please. Yesterday I -- excuse me for interrupting. Yesterday, just to refresh your -- what you said about it, when I asked you if you were familiar not so much with the document, with the content, you indicated that messages of this type were given to you, or you were given information of this type --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not very legible. It says "Dubrovnik, Please convey or transmit to the command of the VPS" - which probably means naval sector - "Boka the following message: Addressed to the command of the naval sector of Boka and the European Mission. We protest most vigorously another violation on your part of the cease-fire perpetrated today between 1445 and 1500 hours by sniper fire from the direction of Bosanka against civilians in the area of Zlatni Potok settlement on Ploce. It is pure good luck that none of them was hurt. Crisis Staff, Dubrovnik." Copies, office of the European Mission in Dubrovnik, another copy to the European Mission in Split and the European Mission in Zagreb. The seal says "Command of the Defence of Municipality of Dubrovnik, number 202/191, date 4 December 1991, Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rudolf, for assisting us. Again, this type of information would have come to your attention, is that what you're indicating, as part of your briefing of what was going on in the area? I'm sorry. Could you --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document previously marked for identification as P161 will now become Exhibit P161. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting you, since the document has already been produced and accepted as evidence, but the Defence is concerned because there is no consistent practice regarding documents that the witness does not recognise as such, but rather, knows something about the content of those documents. You will remember, Your Honour, that with the witness Jokic, we faced situations when the witness Jokic knew the content of certain documents but the Prosecution objected to their introduction because of some shortcoming in the document itself. It is our position that if the witness knows something about the contents of the document, then this same standard should apply to similar situations when documents are produced by the Prosecution. Because when the Defence presented documents when there were certain formal shortcomings and objections, the Prosecution objected to their introduction. In this case, the witness doesn't even remember this particular incident. He only knows that such things happened. We do not object in general to the introduction of such documents, but we want one and -- a unified position to be applied in all such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may recall that there was objection to the production of the documents of Admiral Jokic. You may not have noticed, but when the movement was made by Ms. Somers for this document to come into evidence yesterday, I did not receive it. The witness gave some further evidence this morning, Ms. Somers moved again, I then turned and looked to see whether either of you were going to object, and you did not. I then indicated that it would be received into evidence because there was no objection, as there had been to the documents of Admiral Jokic. You've now objected. Can I indicate, Ms. Somers, that the practice we have been following would not have allowed the admission of this document in the face of objection. I think it's fair to say that there is an objection, and my present view is that we should leave this as marked for identification. Is there anything you would want to put about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would distinguish what my learned colleague was referring to with Admiral Jokic's exhibit, where he said I know part of it. I know part of the content. In this instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the present witness says he knows nothing of the content. That's not a very strong argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In this instance we're asking about incidents where they're briefing -- yesterday there was testimony that their hostilities were not active but that there were briefings. I think that given the other document that was also admitted, it is consistent with what would have been included in a briefing. And the other one, of course, is in the harbour-master's log, it is part of -- it's got a consistent -- it's got a separate corroborative element to it. This one -- I don't know that it also appears in the harbour-master's log. Yes, actually it does, Your Honour. I -- well, before I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't help you. At the moment, the witness, for understandable reasons, has no recollection of the document or of the incident. And you want, in the face of that, to tender it. There is now an objection to it being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think it is difficult to overcome the particular ground, and if that is the case, I will leave it in identified status at this time. But as to tab 8, I believe we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with this document first. I wrongly indicated a moment ago it would now become an exhibit. It remains marked for identification as P161. That is tab 17. And we now turn to tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I think the objection, if I understood it, went only to tab 17, as there is an independent corroboration in -- of the incident from tab 8 on page 6 of the log, and whether the Chamber takes it for the truth of it or not, it's the same information that is contained in the log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe simply that what my learned friend is -- not correct. The harbour-master's log dates from the 5th December onwards. 5th, 6th, the 7th. And the incident mentioned in the document which is in dispute refers to the 8th of November. It says so in the upper left corner in the B/C/S version. It is simply not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, I believe the document that I'm talking about has a 5 December date in tab 8. Tab 8, it is 5 December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 17 is not an exhibit. That's been reversed. Your objection has been upheld. We're now dealing with tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I allow that I have made a mistake perhaps. Document under tab 17 has nothing to do with the document under tab 8. But I understood my colleague is saying that the confirmation of the document under tab 17 is in the document under tab 8. If I understood this wrongly, I apologise to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The only issue, Mr. Petrovic, is whether you object to the introduction of tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we can move along in the harbour-master's log to page 7, please, and ask you, Mr. Rudolf, to take a look at page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And perhaps -- I will indicate to the Chamber that in reviewing the B/C/S and English versions, I have found some shortcomings in the English translation, and I will try to point them out to the Chamber as they arise, as we pass them, pass by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Entry for the 5th of December, the time indicated -- let's see. Have I missed something? Perhaps I have. I may have to go back a minute to get to the original entry. Yes. Before we go to that page, if you flip back to page 1, page 1, where there is an entry for the time frame of 8.15, which would be 8.15 in the morning. Mr. Rudolf, do you see that entry? I'm sorry. Was that a yes? I didn't --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does that indicate that the Argosy II left -- or do you agree that the Argosy II left the town port for Cavtat with the European Community representatives? Would that be the group that you were travelling with to Cavtat for your negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 5th of December. Yes. Yes. That was the ship and that was our group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And returning to page 7, where we had been a moment ago, at the top of page 7 there is an entry for 1216, and it is that -- let's see. For YUX. X is for the Crisis Staff of Croatia. "The Argosy II left Cavtat and is due in the Old Town port in half an hour." Now, is that a communication that would emanate from the forces under the JNA control because of requirements of announcing naval travel?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to announce our arrival, but I believe it was communicated by radio from the ship to the harbour-master. It must have been the time when we were returning from Cavtat to Dubrovnik on the same ship.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Another entry right below it, at 1248, also for -- meant for the Croatians is the Argosy II entered the Old Town port. You can confirm that that again is notice of the arrival of a vessel that would have been subject to a blockade?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Twice, Ms. Somers, you've indicated the call-sign YUX is the Croatians or the Croatian Defence Staff. We have no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is -- Your Honour, it's the context. If you look at the message for -- we can go back and -- I will ask -- I will ask Mr. Rudolf then to explain the source of the message. It's on there and the context pretty much indicates who is who. But let me make that clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
