utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf, if we go back for a moment to the entry on page 3 that we were discussing yesterday, at 10.00, we were talking about plans for the Argosy II on the 9th of December, looking at it on the 5th of December. It says 10.00, it says for YUW from YUX. Now, the message there, is it correct that it is a request to grant passage? YUX is the sender, or requester, seeking passage. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can really not interpret these signs, but in my view, that is a request to the Yugoslav People's Army to grant us safe passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So in your view, who is YUX, if it is a request to the Yugoslav army or forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could be a number of sources. It could be that the request was made by the Crisis Staff of somebody in the civilian authorities of Dubrovnik, but certainly somebody on the Croatian side. However, who specifically, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, who, in your view, since the request appears to be made for YUW, would YUW be? It says from YUX, and you've indicated it is your understanding that that would be the Croatian side. Who would YUW be?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it was one of the commands of the Yugoslav navy, probably in Kumbor or somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And by the context, would that support your conclusion where from YUX there is a request to grant the Argosy II free passage on Monday, the 9th of December? Who controlled the coastal waters at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In order to travel in those waters, of whom would the request have to be made?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appropriate command of the Yugoslav navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have looked at the entries about the Argosy II with your group re-entering the Old Town port, or re-entering Dubrovnik. Can you turn, please, to page 15 - excuse me - page 8. At the entry with the time showing 1825, do you see it at the bottom, pretty low in the bottom? It says for --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. For YUW from YUX. Would you be kind enough to just read the content of it.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Boka VPS, please confirm free and safe passage for the ship Argosy II for its journey tomorrow --" now, I don't understand one of the words here -- "for 10.00 tomorrow in Cavtat. The Dubrovnik municipal Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Dubrovnik Municipal Crisis Staff appears at the bottom of the message.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the English translation reflects "for negotiations scheduled for 10.00 tomorrow." It may be less clear because it's handwritten in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that a message that refers to the planned negotiations for 6 of December? This is on the 5th of December. I'm sorry. You shook your head, but the record doesn't pick up your head-shaking. We need to have a yes or a verbal.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we agreed in Cavtat that we would meet yet again on the following day at 10.00 and sign the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at the next entry of 1930, for YUX, in the interests of time I'll read out what is in the English. "We hereby grant permission and guarantee the Argosy II safe passage from Cavtat (departure time 0900 hours 6 December 1991) until it enters the port of Dubrovnik." Is this a guarantee of safe passage for return, for to and from, to facilitate the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It probably does not say "for return" here, but I believe that that is the way it should be understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The translation I have, "until it enters the port of Dubrovnik." Moving on. 190 --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's all right. Yes. Yes. Safe passage is provided to Cavtat and back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very legible, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do understand, of course. "1900, for YUX from YUW, for the Crisis Staff YUX. We cannot grant your request for introducing a ship line from Sipan to Dubrovnik and back and for starting work on the water pump in Komolac on 6 December 1991, nor can we guarantee the safety of the ship and people. We express our readiness to --" and I have to look at the other version -- "Depending on the results of the negotiations in Cavtat on --" it should read, Your Honours, in the original it says 6 December. The 6 has been left out. I will ask for a correction, which is "on 6 December 1991." If you take a look at the Croatian version, does that -- does this contemplate an understanding that the request is one of the things dealt with or to be dealt with in the 6th of December negotiations? That there's acknowledgment that there are certain provisions that are understood to take place in the 6th of November [sic] negotiations, or to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been agreed in principle already on the 5th, but we hadn't signed anything. And therefore, it remained that we would sign the agreement on the following day, the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now moving on. That is the last entry for the 5th of December. Looking at the entry for 6th of December, it says: "0612 for YUW from YUX." This entry -- can you take a look at it, please, and indicate -- first of all, if the name that is in the B/C/S is Per Hvalkof. It says "name illegible." Actually, I didn't think it was so illegible, I think it was more the handwriting, but you indicated yesterday you knew a person by the name of Per Hvalkof; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, would you please take a look in the Croatian and indicate if indeed you see that name reflected at the bottom of the message --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The protest that is contained in this particular section: "We strongly protest against the bombing of several parts of Dubrovnik that started at about 0600 hours on 6 December 1991 and insist on an immediate cessation of fire. This attack on Dubrovnik is in full opposition to the goodwill you expressed yesterday and the agreement on the unconditional cessation of fire that was signed in Geneva." Then Mr. Hvalkof's name appears for ECMM. Do you concur -- or what is your view about his suggestion that the attack is "in full opposition to the goodwill expressed yesterday?" What is your view on his assertion there? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. On the 5th, a day before that, we had agreed on the cessation of all hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Reading on the next entry, for YUW from YUX, to the Boka VPS command, European Mission: "We strongly protest against the unprovoked strong artillery fire at 0550 hours this morning from the Strincjera and Dubrava areas against the Srdj feature and tank and mortar fire on Dubrovnik." The name indicated, or the term indicated is the Crisis Staff. Is this also a -- is the content of this protest something that you were also familiar with? Did you know about the nature of the attack? Was it conveyed to you? Did you yourself get information?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I was in Dubrovnik then. I didn't find out this early, but around 7.00 we did learn of all these details and we were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Reading on: At 8.12, "One of the Argosy ships has been hit." I think in the Croatian it's easier, but it says at 8.20 -- would you please turn to page 11 of the Croatian and indicate what it says about after "One of the Argosy ships had been hit." Can you look at that on page 11, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What does it say? It's a bit -- the translation didn't make it, but it looks like -- can you read that? It says Argosy and then it has a --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Argosy -- one of the Argosy’s was hit. Argosy -- the fire-fighters can come to the city gates to try to put out the fire. I think that's what it says. Message conveyed. OIC.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Argosy is smoking? Is that the word? Did you say --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. One of the Argosy hit. Argosy -- it's very illegible. Perhaps it does say smoking, smoke coming out of it. But I can say what happened. I saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that one of the Argosy had been hit and set on fire, and then the fire from one of the Argosy ships was transferred to the other one, and then they both burned and sunk. That could be seen very nicely from the Argentina Hotel because both of these ships were in the city harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had the Argosy been used, to your knowledge -- what had the Argosy been used for, to your knowledge, and what was its contemplated use, either the I or the II? There were two Argosy’s. What were the contemplated uses?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that we travelled on this Argosy to Cavtat and from Cavtat, and I treated it as a protected parliamentary ship.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not it had any indicia of either a mission or something that would show its status as you suggested it was protected; any type of banner, symbol, flag?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we set off for Cavtat, I talked to them and I asked them to put a banner up. There was a flag up there, but I'm not sure whether it was white or blue. I told the commander and he said: Yes, we have got a flag. And it shows that this is a ship where negotiators are on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just ask my learned colleague to denote the exact time. Was it when the ship was travelling from Dubrovnik to Cavtat with the negotiators on board, or is it the time when it was anchored in the Dubrovnik harbour?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could address -- if I may ask Mr. Rudolf to address this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it both when it was at -- in port, as well as at sail, that it had some indication? And if you can only answer one part of it, please do.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was at sail, I know that it was marked. But when it was in port, I couldn't tell, I couldn't see from the hotel, because it's pretty far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on to the next entry for -- it says 9.55 for YUX from YUW. For the Crisis Staff, for Davorin Rudolf, from the Boka VPS. And there seems to be a question about one bit of the English, but: "We are making an enormous effort to stop the clashes --" it looks like "caused by shooting from Srdj and Lapad. We request you to intervene immediately to stop the clashes at 1115 hours today. We propose that the meeting be postponed until 1200 hours today." First of all, what meeting -- Boka VPS. What meeting, to your knowledge, is being referred to that would have taken place at 1200 -- or is being sought for postponement until 1200 hours?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first we had an agreement on the 5th of December with regard to a meeting that was supposed to be held in Cavtat on the 6th at 10.00. When Admiral Jokic and I spoke, and I think I also sent a radiogram because of the attack on Dubrovnik, we kept postponing the meeting to 12.00, and I think then 1.30. It depended, you see, on whether there would be a cease-fire or not. So I think it pertained to the meeting between us and Admiral Jokic, because we postponed it several times. And finally he called and said that we -- that he was supposed to travel to Belgrade at 2.00. So technically, the meeting could not have been held on that day, and therefore, it was not. He postponed it because at 2.00, at 1400 hours, he went to Belgrade, so he said that we indeed could not meet on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It was your observation or perception that despite the fact that it had to be postponed, that Admiral Jokic was trying to have the meeting take place and that perhaps -- well, that's part one. Was it your perception?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, the circumstances -- if we keep going, and I will return to any conversations you may have had with Admiral Jokic in a moment, but entry at 10.20 on page 12, from -- for YUW from YUX. And your name is underneath that entry. Would you be good enough, please, to read it.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We accept a strict cease-fire as of 1115 hours. For practical reasons, we cannot come to the meeting by 12.00, so we propose that the meeting be held at 1330 hours, or rather, as soon as possible. D. Rudolf."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is that in fact a communication you made?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving down to one of the entries under 1027 for YUX, where it says: "For D. Rudolf. Admiral Jokic asks Mr. D. Rudolf to come to the meeting as soon as possible because later the admiral has pressing official engagements. The admiral requests an urgent reply from Mr. D. Rudolf." Does that correctly reflect what was relayed to you about Admiral Jokic's time frame?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he later sent a radiogram saying that he had to go to Belgrade. And he exactly confirmed that he had to go at 1400 hours and therefore we could not meet. I wanted for us to meet as soon as possible, due to the situation, and I had the impression that Admiral Jokic wanted us to meet as soon as possible too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The official -- the pressing official engagements and the time frame of 1330, does that -- did you interpret that in light of his later communication to mean that it was the Belgrade meeting that was the official -- the pressing official engagement?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Later?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there's another radiogram where he says that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on. The 1045 entry, for YUW from YUX for Davorin Rudolf to Admiral Jokic at the Boka VPS. "Since both of the Argosy ships have been hit and burned, we would like to come on a Split Port Authority ship marked I ST 3 with Port Authority written on the side. Please confirm the safe passage of the ship from port of Gruz to Cavtat and back. I believe that the Split Port Authority ship was not hit and I cannot verify it at the moment. The proposal for a cease-fire as of 1115 hours has been accepted. The Split Port Authority ship was also hit or damaged. Please let us know how we can come to Cavtat in that case."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Somers please be asked to read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters for reading so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again it is D. Rudolf, but there is a PS. "I wish to stress once again that the Port Authority ship would depart from the port of Gruz. Please confirm safe passage." In fact, did you ever depart from the port of Gruz that day on the Port Authority vessel? Did you have a meeting that day with Admiral Jokic in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not on that day. We did not have a meeting on that day and we did not sail out of the port of Gruz either. Allow me to explain. In Dubrovnik there is the city port facing east - or towards the border with Montenegro, to be clearer - and the port of Gruz, which is on the west side. At that moment, our Port Authority ship was in Gruz and we did not know whether it had been hit or not. That is why I worded it this way. But in response to your question: No, we did not have any direct meeting on that day with Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at the entry 1105, it is for YUW from YUX, addressed to the Boka command and the European Mission. I will go quickly through it for the record, but I want to ask you a couple of questions at the end of it. At 550 hours: "Tank fire from the positions at Strincjera, Bosanka and Zarkovica, a company backed by infantry began an attack on the positions of defence forces of the Republic of Croatia at Srdj. At the same time opening mortar and machine-gun fire on all parts of the town. The defence forces of the Republic of Croatia responded only after the infantry and tanks came within 200 metres of Srdj. We deny carrying out any acts of provocation or activities from Srdj and Lapad that would have been a cause for the cease-fire violations. We declare with full responsibility that the allegations of the activities of our forces have been fabricated in order to justify the attempt to take Srdj. We have stopped further activity --" and perhaps you can help us in the Croatian. "We expect true compliance with the cease-fire and the withdrawal of your forces to their starting positions. At this moment, your forces are firing on the Dubrovnik municipal Crisis Staff headquarters, Srdj, and the town of Dubrovnik." And it is -- there is an indication of the municipal Crisis Staff below it. Are you familiar with where the Dubrovnik municipal Crisis Staff headquarters were at this date?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the city municipality, that is, within the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you made aware at any time, let's say up until 6.00 in the morning, of any protest lodged by anyone on the JNA, your partners in negotiating on the JNA side, about Croatian attacks against JNA forces in the area of -- well, on the hill where Srdj, Bosanka, that area, are? Any attacks at all in the early morning hours of the 6th, maybe the cusp of the 5th to the early morning hours of the 6th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I checked that later. Actually, I was asleep at the time. The shooting woke me up later, but I asked how all of it had happened. The commander of the defence of Dubrovnik told me that there was no shooting from our side and that there was nothing done to provoke an attack from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- moving along in the entries. 1128 -- on page 15, there's an entry for 1128 hours to Admiral Jokic, and it is at the end, which is at page 17 - it's a bit lengthy - it is from -- it is indicated that it is from yourself. Can you please perhaps tell us where you were when these communications were being made. Where were you physically located, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Argentina Hotel, or actually, this is a small annex building by the hotel. That's where we all were throughout that day, the 6th of December. The Argentina Hotel would be my answer. Orsula is the name of the annex, but all of it is a single hotel. So it is all one facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I note that on page 16, when you were in the process of explaining about trying to get to Cavtat, you indicate: "We cannot get out into the street because the attack is still in progress although it has decreased in intensity. I have been informed that troop movements towards Srdj are continuing despite the cease-fire agreement." Now, in this indication, troop movements by which troops are being referred to? What did you intend to convey there? Whose troops?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The troops of the Yugoslav People's Army. This is 11.28, so after the cessation of hostilities at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Continuing: "The old part of the town has been heavily bombarded. Fires can be seen in several places and both ships sailing to Cavtat have been hit. They are still burning in the harbour. Machine-gun fire and occasional mine explosions are heard from Zarkovica." And I believe that in the Croatian -- if you could take a look, please, in the Croatian version, because it says, after the term "Zarkovica" "three words illegible." Would you be good enough to look at page 16 in Croatian and try to assist us with what comes next. It says: "I heard from Zarkovica..." and then right after that.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As I'm writing this." "From Zarkovica, as I am writing this, machine-gun fire can be heard." So the three words are "dok ovo pisem," "as I'm writing this."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "The reports of destruction on the Stradun near the Old Town hall are coming in. Two shells apparently hit St. Blaise's church. A building in the Old Town is burning. I believe that you personally are making every effort to secure a cease-fire. Can you stress once again that the negotiations are under way." And there is a correction in the next line. If you could look in the Croatian, if you'd be good enough, perhaps, because we noted in reviewing that it was confusing because it is incorrect. "Can you stress once again that the negotiations are under way and that the building in which --" if you could help us with that sentence. How should it be correctly interpreted?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking about that, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Page 17.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "Can you stress once again that the negotiations are under way," and then it makes reference to the building in which, it says, "negotiations are taking place." Is that what is really written in Croatian, that negotiations -- or what is actually there, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it says: "It should be pointed out that negotiations are under way."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a word that's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does it make reference --

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The building where the negotiators are was hit and the parliamentary ship was hit and destroyed and that we got guarantees from the JNA for free passage to attend negotiations and that since written history has existed, negotiations took place with negotiators being fully protected. It is 1210 now and occasional shots are still being fired from Zarkovica. Please make further efforts to ensure that the negotiations are completed and put an immediate stop to this totally irrational situation. D. Rudolf." And then it says: "As things stand now, we practically cannot go into the street, let alone to the ship. I would ask you to propose a new time --" it's hardly legible again -- "because obviously we cannot get to Cavtat in time."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the assistance, Mr. Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just point out, then, to Your Honours that on page 17, where it says at the very -- it would be the third line, under "Details of Work," that the building in which, instead of "negotiations are taking place," "the building in which the negotiators are staying has been hit."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what building would that be referring to, Mr. Rudolf, where the negotiators were staying? What building would that have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hotel Argentina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at page 18, the entry for 1145 hours, for YUW from YUX. Just one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, before we move on, on that particular point. In the passage you just read where there was a description of what was occurring in the Old Town, with the Old Town coming under fire, are you familiar -- or do you know if in the course of the attack on the 6th of December, was there any indication or protest to the Croatian representatives or the group with which you found yourself, protest by the JNA of any military activity coming from the Old Town, any outgoing fire from the Old Town? Was there any protest made to your side? In other words, fire coming from within the Old Town, was there any protest made?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your first question: I was first informed of this by General Strugar in a radiogram he sent at 4.30 p.m. It was his interpretation. He said the Croatian forces had provoked the attack and that despite the cease-fire, they continued shooting from the Old Town and that those forces had in fact set fire to the Old Town themselves. I believe you have this radiogram in the original and you can read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I just ask: That is a response you're referring to which we'll get to, but I am talking about your reading entries where it is indicated that the Old Town is under attack. Had there prior to that time, from the time the attack began until let's say these entries are indicated, been any protest that you are aware of by JNA as to outgoing fire from the Old Town? I'm sorry, your answer was?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, picking up at page 18, the entry for 1145 hours. This is a message for Minister Davorin Rudolf at the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff from the Boka VP -- it says VPO perhaps VPS. Would you be good enough, please, to read that response, read that message. If you care to do it.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, Minister Davorin Rudolf, at the VPO Boka. Dear Minister, I express my sincere regret with this difficult situation and incident. It was not our order, because it would have never crossed my mind to do such a thing. General Kadijevic has sent you and the European Mission in Dubrovnik a message, saying that he had ordered an urgent investigation to establish our responsibility and identify the culprit for this incident. At the same time, we believe that you, on your part, will establish your part of the responsibility in order to shed full light on the circumstances of the incidents of last night and this morning. He called me to come to Belgrade at 1400 hours today, so I will not be able to continue my talks with you today. "I propose the following: That we resume our talks at 1200 hours tomorrow after my return from Belgrade. "Second, to accept our proposal for an unconditional cessation of fire in the entire --" I can't read this word very easily. It probably says "operative zone." "Dubrovnik to Ston. "3. The daily service from Cavtat to Dubrovnik should be opened" - and here it probably says "Gruz, Mokosica" - "and Dubrovnik to the islands twice a week." So it says to open the daily service from Cavtat to Dubrovnik, Gruz, Mokosica, Zaton, and Dubrovnik to the islands twice a week. Four -- here again we have an illegible word. "Ships should be checked in the port of Gruz." Five, that sides or parties -- I cannot read this handwriting easily. "That our parties encircled units," it says, "and the combat elements positioned along the forward line should withdraw without leaving any combat elements." Six: "The roads leading out of the town, including the one leading to Ston, should be reopened." Seven: "The blockade of the town should be fully lifted and the weapons threatening the town should be withdrawn out of range. Members of the armed forces who came into the town should be evacuated on first available ships." Eight: "We can discuss other problems in Cavtat at 1200 hours on the 7th of December, 1991." Postscript: "Once again, we express our regret over this incident and hope that we will be able to overcome this. Vice Admiral Miodrag Jokic."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it your understanding, or can you indicate what your understanding was from this message as to what Admiral Jokic cited as the cause or the source of the attack, the reason for the attack? Let me rephrase that. I withdraw that question. It's perhaps too difficult to approach. Was it your understanding from this message that there was an admission by Admiral Jokic of the involvement of the units of the JNA with respect to starting this attack?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes. And he says here, making reference even to Kadijevic, who was the minister of defence in Yugoslavia, that he ordered an investigation in order to establish who is responsible for the incident and to find the culprit. And of course, he says that we on our part should also conduct an investigation and see if there is any responsibility on our part. And you haven't asked me this, but I wish to say that this radiogram was very important to us. I read it to the people of Dubrovnik over Radio Dubrovnik. I'm not speaking about the naval radio station but about the regular Radio Dubrovnik, broadcasting regular programmes. It was indeed very important. That's how I saw it and how all the people of Dubrovnik saw it. He expressed here his regret over this difficult situation and incident, as he called it. He says it was not done on my orders and it would have never crossed my mind. I would have never thought of doing such a thing. We received this radiogram as a very important one, and it had a great psychological impact in a positive sense, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you confirm that based on the situation on the ground when you and Admiral Jokic left Cavtat the day before, the 5th, that this situation was not contemplated, that this incident would not have been contemplated?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one among us, not only did not think along those lines; moreover, I can tell that you it came as a great relief to us. We conveyed this explanation to the people and it gave us hope. None of us expected, even when this attack started and when I got down and saw with my own eyes what was going on, I couldn't believe my eyes. I later talked to a representative of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, and I could not fathom that an agreement we had reached could be violated because officers of the JNA were educated people. At that moment, I did not feel that my life was in danger, but I felt humiliated, devastated, completely despondent, because it seemed absolutely unbelievable to me that a thing like that could happen because the first thing we agreed on in Cavtat was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You said that you read this to the people of Dubrovnik over radio. Were -- in your estimation, did you find -- how did you see the people of Dubrovnik reacting to this attack on the morning of the 6th?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, we were staying at a hotel and we were in the hotel at that time. We were unable to leave Hotel Argentina. Let me explain. To the east of the hotel, you see clearly all the way up to a hill called Zarkovica, and from this place Zarkovica, fire was opened on that road between us and Zarkovica, and there was no other way to go out into the streets of Dubrovnik. And all these people around us, and of course we were in constant contact with the Crisis Staff, with the mayor, with the president of the Executive Board, we were in permanent contact with the commander of the Dubrovnik defence, because the telephone lines continued working all the time at the hotel. We had electricity. We were able to watch TV, because the hotel was equipped with a power unit and generator. And I can tell you that this telegram, this message, came to us as a very comforting one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you something? There has been a suggestion that perhaps in the course of what you've just described, you made a reference to the Old Town. Did you -- as I don't see it in the transcript, was there a reference made in the Old Town in what you have just said? If so, it has not made its way to the transcript. And if not, just indicate.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when I say "Old Town," I mean the part of Dubrovnik which is walled in by the ramparts. Around the Old Town was the municipality. That's where the Crisis Staff was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Because I just wanted -- it didn't seem to show up, and I'd been informed that it had been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness did not say what the record says: "around the Old Town was the municipality." The meaning of the witness was that the municipality, the town hall, was in the Old Town. When he says "municipality," he probably means the town hall. That's at least how I understood him, the way he put it in B/C/S. Inside the ramparts of the Old Town was the municipality, literally speaking, meaning the town hall. That's what I understood the witness as saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you confirm that? Is that what you intended? If my counsel -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The building and the members of the Crisis Staff were there, that is, the building facing the St. Blaise church.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, there is a mention in -- on page 18 in Admiral Jokic's communique to you at, the bottom. It says, when it's discussing establishing responsibility: "At the same time, we believe that you will also establish your part of responsibility in order to shed full light on the circumstances of the incidents last night and this morning." Now, did -- from the perspective of the Croatian representatives, was there perceived to be any reason to investigate anything in terms of culpability by the Croatians? What was the view?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Look, Dubrovnik was literally in a mousetrap. You should have been there and seen what it actually looks like. It was besieged from up there in the hills and it was under blockade from the sea. In the military sense, Dubrovnik had no -- presented no interest at all. It was very poorly armed and had a very small number of soldiers. What kind of person in that situation would have tried to cause any provocation? Second thing: Everybody in Dubrovnik knew that negotiations were under way, and everybody was expecting an agreement to be signed the next day. In that kind of situation, in a town which had no electricity, no water, where people were going hungry, suffering from cold, a town in a terribly difficult situation, who on earth on the Croatian side would have been crazy enough to provoke an attack? And third: I must say that I asked our commander of the Dubrovnik defence, Lieutenant Colonel Nojko Marinovic, whether anything had been done on our part to provoke an attack, and he told me definitely not. But for you to understand what the situation was like, I have to tell you this: Nojko Marinovic is a soldier. We were ministers of the Croatian government. When he was coming to report to us, he came with a marching step. He would stand at attention before us and act as a real soldier. And he told us, very decisively, very positively: "No." I believed him, not only because of what he was saying but because the whole situation, that it was inconceivable really that anyone on the Croatian side could have done anything to provoke that situation that happened on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How would you have characterised or how did you characterise the defence of Dubrovnik? And I mean would you have characterised it as a strong defence, a weak defence? What was your view, as having been sent as a negotiator and having come from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the report was made to us on what was going on, especially when we received a report on the status of defence by Nojko Marinovic, who was lieutenant colonel at the time, we understood that we were militarily completely inferior, poorly armed, and had very few soldiers. And regarding the number of soldiers, various figures were mentioned during the negotiations. General Jokic at one point mentioned 15.000 soldiers, and mercenaries even, as he put it. However, that was far from the truth. There were relatively few soldiers, armed, I would say, inadequately. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you comment on the arming? Was there -- was Zagreb assisting in providing whatever needs Dubrovnik requested of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Far from it. First of all, Zagreb could not have done that, even if they wanted to. And for all that to arrive to Dubrovnik, if Zagreb sent 100 units, say, 10 would actually arrive. Because on the way to Dubrovnik, everybody would take for their own defence whatever they needed, and relatively little would reach Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on page 75, line 19, something is missing, namely, a reference to the fact that General Jokic mentioned those 15.000 soldiers and mercenaries at negotiations in Cavtat. If I'm not mistaken, this is missing from the record and the witness actually said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, he did, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Also, I would assume that it would not be General Jokic, but Admiral Jokic, if that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Am I fair to assume that you had intended to say Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, when you mentioned sending units but that things didn't make it because along the way they were taken, are you referring to weaponry, supply of weapons from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean everybody. It was a very chaotic situation. Dubrovnik, as I said, was under blockade from both land and sea. The Yugoslav People's Army had occupied everything up to the Neretva River, that is, about 70 to 80 kilometres to the west, towards Split, so that serious weaponry could not even have been delivered to Dubrovnik. I am not a soldier myself, and I do not know much about those things, and my impressions are, I would say, those of a layman. And as for the objection of this gentleman here, of course, I haven't even begun to tell you all the details from the negotiations in Cavtat. I have managed only to cover the most important things. And I don't know, Counsel, what you meant when you said: Did he actually mention 15.000 or not? Those were talks between General -- between Mr. Kriste and General Jokic, and if you need me to give you more detail about that, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again, I assume when you refer to Jokic, you mean Admiral Jokic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVORIN RUDOLF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always mean exclusively Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As opposed to General Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Somers, I'm afraid we have run five minutes over what was a deadline in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't realise. I thought it was 12.30. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was 12.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And time is now getting critical for me. I'm sorry, Dr. Rudolf, but as I indicated briefly yesterday, we must bring to an end the evidence of today. I hope you don't treat this as disrespectful. It just happens that these days are very disturbed days, this Wednesday and this Thursday, in our programme, and it means, I'm afraid, that you are being put to inconvenience. We apologise. But we must stop now, and we resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. And as I indicated, the morning itself will be cut short by planned evidence which we will be receiving from other witnesses according to a timetable set nearly a month ago. So we apologise in advance. We will now adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
